title: Design a Parking Lot — Vehicle types (car/bike/truck), ParkingSpot sizes, ParkingFloor, entry/exit gates, ticket system, payment, find nearest available spot.

s1_definition.profdef: A parking lot design is an object-oriented model of a multi-floor facility that assigns an incoming vehicle to a compatible spot, issues a ticket at entry, tracks occupancy, and computes a fee at exit. The core abstractions are Vehicle, ParkingSpot, ParkingFloor, Ticket, and a PaymentStrategy.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the parking lot as the vault of National Bank of India where lockers come in three sizes. When Rajesh arrives with a small item he gets a small locker, Priya with a large item gets a large locker, the clerk writes a slip (ticket) noting the entry time, and when they leave the cashier charges by the hours used. The parking lot assigns spots exactly like the bank assigns lockers.
s1_definition.oneliner: A parking lot assigns the nearest compatible spot, issues a ticket, and charges by duration at exit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A parking lot design is an object-oriented model of a multi-floor facility that assigns an incoming vehicle to a compatible spot, issues a ticket at entry, tracks occupancy, and computes a fee at exit. The core abstractions are Vehicle, ParkingSpot, ParkingFloor, Ticket, and a PaymentStrategy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the parking lot as the vault of National Bank of India where lockers come in three sizes. When Rajesh arrives with a small item he gets a small locker, Priya with a large item gets a large locker, the clerk writes a slip (ticket) noting the entry time, and when they leave the cashier charges by the hours used. The parking lot assigns spots exactly like the bank assigns lockers.

**One line to remember:** A parking lot assigns the nearest compatible spot, issues a ticket, and charges by duration at exit.

sections.s2_technical:
The `Vehicle` hierarchy models size through an enum rather than deep inheritance, because a bike, car, and truck differ only in the spot size they need. A `ParkingSpot` has a size and an occupied flag. A `ParkingFloor` holds a list of spots and knows how to find the nearest free spot for a given size.

The `ParkingLot` is the orchestrator: on entry it finds a spot, marks it occupied, and returns a `Ticket` with entry time. On exit it computes duration, applies a `FeeStrategy`, and frees the spot. Using a strategy for fees lets the lot support flat, hourly, or dynamic surge pricing without editing the lot code, which is the Open/Closed principle.

```java
ParkingSpot spot = floor.findNearestSpot(VehicleType.CAR);
```

Finding the nearest spot is a simple scan here, but in production you would keep per-size priority queues keyed by distance so the lookup is logarithmic. Thread safety matters because two cars can arrive at the same instant, so spot allocation must be synchronized or use atomic compare-and-set on the occupied flag.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a staff parking facility. Rajesh drives a car and Priya a bike, and both arrive at the morning rush. The system must hand each the nearest compatible spot without double-allocating. This is exactly the entry and spot-finding logic.

Problem 2 — At evening exit the facility must charge fairly by hours parked, and management wants to switch from flat to hourly pricing without a rewrite. This is exactly what a fee strategy provides.

The code defines `VehicleType`, `ParkingSpot`, `ParkingFloor`, `Ticket`, a `FeeStrategy`, and a `ParkingLot` orchestrator, with a demo parking and exiting both vehicles.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh arrives in a car, Priya on a bike, floor F1 has one car spot and one bike spot.

Step 1: `lot.park(CAR,...)` scans floors, `findNearestSpot(CAR)` returns F1-C1 and marks it occupied, returning ticket TKT-1. Step 2: `lot.park(BIKE,...)` returns F1-B1 and ticket TKT-2. Step 3: at exit, `exit(rajesh)` sets the exit time, frees F1-C1, and `HourlyFee` computes at least one hour at 50 rupees. Step 4: the same happens for Priya. The spots are now free for the next vehicles.

```
Oct 31 22:07 INFO PARK: MH01-RAJESH parked at F1-C1
Oct 31 22:07 INFO PARK: MH02-PRIYA parked at F1-B1
Oct 31 22:07 INFO PARK: Exit TKT-1 fee=50
Oct 31 22:07 INFO PARK: Exit TKT-2 fee=50
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Parking Lot ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: FeeStrategy (hourly/flat/surge)         │
  │   WHY: change pricing without editing ParkingLot  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Floor finds spots; Lot orchestrates; Fee prices│
  │ O: new pricing = new FeeStrategy impl             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────┐ owns  ┌───────────────┐ owns ┌─────────────┐
  │  ParkingLot  │◆─────▶│ ParkingFloor  │◆────▶│ ParkingSpot │
  │ - floors     │       │ + findNearest │      │ - size      │
  │ - feeStrategy│◇┐     │   Spot(type)  │      │ - occupied  │
  │ + park()     │ │uses └───────────────┘      └─────────────┘
  │ + exit()     │ └─▶ FeeStrategy (interface)
  └──────────────┘

  State: Spot: FREE → OCCUPIED → FREE
  Call Chain:
  1. park(CAR) → floor.findNearestSpot(CAR) → mark occupied → Ticket
  2. exit(ticket) → free spot → FeeStrategy.fee(duration)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When I design a parking lot, I model it as a small set of cohesive classes rather than one giant manager. The core entities are Vehicle with a type that captures size, ParkingSpot that carries a size and an occupied flag, ParkingFloor that owns its spots and knows how to find the nearest free compatible spot, Ticket that records the entry time, and a ParkingLot orchestrator that ties them together at the entry and exit gates.

On entry, the lot walks its floors and asks each floor to find the nearest free spot of the right size. I make that allocation thread safe, because at a busy facility two vehicles can arrive at the same instant and I must never hand the same spot to both. Once a spot is reserved I issue a ticket stamped with the entry time.

On exit, I compute the parked duration and apply a fee strategy. I deliberately pull pricing into a strategy interface so the facility can switch from flat to hourly to surge pricing by adding a new class, never touching the orchestrator — that is the Open/Closed principle paying off directly in a feature request.

For scale I would replace the linear spot scan with per-size priority queues keyed by distance so lookups stay fast even with thousands of spots, and I would cache free-spot counts per floor in Redis for the display boards. I always relate it to my banking work: assigning a parking spot is structurally the same as assigning a vault locker at National Bank of India, where size compatibility, safe concurrent allocation, and duration-based charging are exactly the concerns I handle.
